title: How to Set Up a Sick-Day Station Before Cold and Flu Season
description: Make one sick-day bin before anyone gets the sniffles: what to put in it, where to keep it and how to stay stocked without thinking about it.
intro:
It's 2 a.m. Someone has a fever. You're digging through three cabinets for the thermometer, finding six empty tissue boxes and a bottle of something that expired before the pandemic.

When someone is sick, nobody has the energy to hunt. Least of all our brains, which already struggle with finding things on a *good* day.

So let's do the hunting now, while everyone's well. One sick-day station, set up in about 15 minutes, and cold season gets a little less chaotic. (Quick note: this is about being organized, not medical advice. Ask your doctor or pharmacist what's right for your family.)

sections.heading: Step 1: Pick one bin
sections.body:
Grab a clear bin with a handle. A handle matters: when someone's sick, you want to carry the whole kit to the couch or bedside in one trip.

Label it big: **SICK DAY.** It should be the most obvious bin in the house.

sections.heading: Step 2: Gather what you already have
sections.body:
Walk through the house and pull together the stuff you reach for when someone's under the weather:

- Thermometer (and spare batteries for it)
- Tissues
- Any medicine your family uses, checked for dates
- Cough drops or throat lozenges
- Lip balm
- Hand sanitizer
- A small notepad and pen

That notepad is the secret weapon. Write down what was taken and when. Tired brains don't remember, and a written log beats guessing at 3 a.m.

sections.heading: Step 3: Toss expired stuff
sections.body:
Check every date. Expired medicine goes to a pharmacy take-back bin or a local drop-off, not the trash. Put the bag by the door or in the car so it actually leaves.

While you're at it, write the earliest expiry date on a sticky note on the bin lid. That's your next check-in date.

sections.heading: Step 4: Add the comfort layer
sections.body:
Sick days are about comfort as much as anything. Keep a second, smaller basket or a shelf nearby with:

- A couple of electrolyte drink packets
- Crackers or plain snacks that keep well
- A reusable water bottle with a straw
- A heat pack or a cozy blanket
- A phone charger with a long cable

Anything that saves a trip to the store on a bad day earns its spot.

sections.heading: Step 5: Keep it where you'll find it
sections.body:
Pick one spot and tell everyone. A shelf in the linen closet or a high kitchen cabinet works well, safely out of reach of little kids and away from bathroom steam.

If you have a family command center, add "Sick kit: linen closet, top shelf" to it. Future-you, half asleep, will be grateful.

sections.heading: Step 6: Restock on autopilot
sections.body:
Here's where our brains usually slip: we use the last tissue and forget to replace it. Two easy fixes:

- Keep a **"used it, need it" sticky note** inside the lid. Whoever uses the last of something writes it down.
- Set a calendar reminder every three months to open the bin and check.

You can also add tissues and cough drops to a recurring grocery order, so they show up without a decision.

sections.heading: Bonus: a go-bag for appointments
sections.body: Keep a zip pouch in the bin with a copy of insurance cards, a list of everyone's medicines and allergies, and your doctor's phone number. When you need to head out to an appointment fast, grab the pouch and go.

outro:
Fifteen minutes now saves a lot of 2 a.m. searching later. One bin, one spot, one sticky note for restocking.

For more small setups that make home life easier, *The Messy Brain Home Reset* walks you through one zone a day for seven days.
